title: Gentoo Linux Benchmark Analysis vs Other Operating Systems
text:
I have been using Gentoo Linux since some some time around 2005 on various platforms, and for different purposes.
As for myself, I have almost always trusted the default settings mentioned in the handbook, i.e. the “conservative” CFLAGS parameters, using -march=native to optimize for the given processor architecture, and rarely venturing further into “optimization” land.
However, throughout forums, Reddit, chat channels, and other places, there’s been constant debates on what “the best” optimization flags are (or should be), with many swearing by their magical incantations of compilers, compiler flags, and linkers, to produce seemingly fantastic, but vague, claims of performance gains.
I hadn’t given much thought as to how my own systems should be optimized, until I got an Intel NUC, with a 12th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-1260P processor. This processor has differentiated performance (“P-Cores”) and efficient-cores (“E-Cores”) in Intel’s lingo, and sometimes fail to produce binaries that can execute on all cores with automatic -march=native settings. So I started digging deeper to find out exactly what compiler flags I should use on a given architecture, and which ones actually made a difference performance-wise.
The GCC optimization article on the Gentoo Wiki also provided some interesting food for thought.
So how would I actually test this systematically? I set up virtual machines in libvirt on two of my machines to find out, in general terms, what would produce the most optimized system, with everything else (installed software, kernel versions, filesystems, schedulers, etc.) being the same.
These two machines are
I ended up with a set of Gentoo Linux VM:s, each with different combinations of CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS, hardened/unhardened profiles, link-time optimization (LTO), profile-guided optimization (PGO) (where applicable), and Graphite loop optimizations. I rebuilt all of these systems from the ground up (emerge --emptytree) and kept them updated continously over a period of several months in order to properly log compile times, etc.
Optimization is usually a set of trade-off between simplicity, stability, compilation time, execution time, and maintainability. As an example, if a program takes an extra 20 minutes to compile every time you install or upgrade it, and the gain in performance each time you use it is measured in seconds, it might not be worthwhile to optimize it from a technical perspective. Many, however, have a complementary – lets call it a psychological perspective – and derives peace-of-mind from knowing their system is optimized, and uses ALL of their processor. So I knew I needed to be able to compare compilation times, and cross-reference them with any performance data I could derive.
As previously mentioned, the NUC has differentiated cores, which means that the compiler cannot reliably use -march=native to resolve the correct parameters for the CPU. Instead, on that platform resolve-march-native resolves the actual (usable) compiler flags.
This article compares benchmark outcomes across supported operating systems, with focused analysis of Gentoo tuning choices (CFLAGS, PGO, LTO, Graphite).
The real hostnames have been replaced by names from Greek Mythology so we can refer to them later in this article.
The virtual machines are run on app-emulation/libvirt-12.0.0/app-emulation/qemu-10.2.2 through an Ansible-based harness that provisions and collects the benchmark data.

title: Gentoo Linux Benchmark Analysis vs Other Operating Systems
text:
How the Benchmarks Are Performed
The benchmark suite is executed by the Ansible role roles/run_benchmarks, which prepares each VM, runs benchmark categories, and writes raw JSON artifacts for every host. Most workloads are measured with Hyperfine-style repeated command timing, with category outputs stored as one JSON file per category.
To reduce noise, the workflow applies a normalization/denormalization pass around benchmark execution. This keeps host state and scheduling more consistent between runs and avoids permanent benchmark-side changes after completion.

title: Gentoo Linux Benchmark Analysis vs Other Operating Systems
text:
How Data Is Collected
Each host writes to benchmarks/results/<host>/:

metadata.json with host/build context (OS, compiler flags, profile, tool versions, platform details).
Category result files with per-command timing data (mean, stddev, command string).
Optional benchmark notes where present.

This article loads those files through scripts/benchmarks_article_data.py, converts them to long-form rows, applies optional hostname anonymization, and then derives aggregate comparisons (cross-OS and Gentoo tuning-focused).

Values lower than peers indicate faster execution for this benchmark corpus.

title: Gentoo Linux Benchmark Analysis vs Other Operating Systems
text:
Per-Category Deep Dives
Each category section starts with a description of what the workload measures and why it matters, followed by a cross-OS comparison chart, a Gentoo-specific tuning chart, and qualitative interpretation. All stored metrics are wall-clock times in seconds (from Hyperfine), so lower is always better for every chart below. Where a benchmark conceptually measures throughput (e.g. crypto MB/s, memory bandwidth), the note in each section explains the relationship between the stored time and the underlying throughput concept.


Bash Shell Performance








Note



What this measures: Profiles the bash interpreter across four micro-benchmarks relevant to build-system workloads: raw binary start/exit overhead (no rc files), integer arithmetic via (( )) in tight loops, string concatenation with +=, and global pattern substitution ${s//x/y}. Build systems for Autoconf-based projects and Gentoo ebuilds generate thousands of bash invocations; small per-invocation costs compound across a full rebuild.

Gentoo tuning interpretation (lower is better, host-level median): The fastest result in this category comes from LTO:on | PGO:on | Graphite:off at 0.012seconds. Compare this against compile-time cost and maintainability before treating it as globally optimal.

Tip



Analysis hint: Startup overhead dominates short scripts. PGO on bash measurably reduces startup latency by improving branch prediction for the interpreter’s hot dispatch paths. Arithmetic and string-substitution results are less sensitive to compiler flags than the raw startup cost.




Caveats: Category-level winners are not universal winners. Hardware differences, package versions, microarchitecture behavior, and benchmark command mix can shift results. Use this deep-dive together with compile-time and maintenance trade-offs before choosing production defaults.

Per-Category Dimension Effects


The heatmap below shows the spread (ratio of slowest to fastest) for each dimension within each category. Higher values indicate greater impact of that dimension on that category.


                            
                                            


Interpretation and Caveats








Warning



Key Caveats:

Confounders: The dimension values are not orthogonal—hosts with -march=native may also differ in optimization level, LTO, PGO, or Graphite settings. This analysis shows association, not causation.
Stability: Benchmark results are influenced by hardware (CPU, cache, thermal throttling), system load, kernel version, package versions, and other factors beyond CFLAGS.
Limited sample size: If a host uses only one value for a dimension (e.g., all samples have lto_mode=off), that dimension cannot be evaluated within that host.
Category bias: Some categories may be more sensitive to certain optimizations (e.g., crypto to LTO), while others show little variation.
Interaction effects: The combined effect of multiple flags may not be the sum of individual effects.

Conclusion: Use these results to form hypotheses about which dimensions might affect your workload, then validate by profiling on representative hardware with controlled experiments.
